cse-2025-1-cs-17.approach: Read the figure as two independent 2-to-1 multiplexers feeding the two ALU inputs, then list every combination of the two select lines. Each option is just a question about which combinations exist.
cse-2025-1-cs-17.given:
| ALU input | Source chosen by | Choices |
|---|---|---|
| left | Mux_A (select RA/immediate) | RA or a 32-bit immediate |
| right | Mux_B (select RB/immediate) | RB or a 32-bit immediate |

The ALU result is written to RZ.

steps.title: What each multiplexer can deliver
steps.body:
Mux_A has two data inputs, **RA** and a **32-bit immediate**, and its own select line. Mux_B likewise has **RB** and a **separate 32-bit immediate**, with its own select line. Their outputs are the ALU's two operands.

Because the two select lines are independent, the data path can realise $2 \times 2 = 4$ operand combinations.

steps.title: Enumerate the four select combinations
steps.body:
| Mux_A | Mux_B | ALU computes |
|---|---|---|
| RA | RB | register op register |
| RA | imm | register op immediate |
| imm | RB | immediate op register |
| imm | imm | immediate op immediate |

Every row is reachable just by setting the two select lines.

steps.title: Check each option against the table
steps.body:
- (A) two registers: row 1 ✓
- (B) one register + one immediate: rows 2 and 3 ✓
- (C) two immediates: row 4 ✓ — each multiplexer has its own immediate input
- (D) says the path can **only** do register + immediate, but rows 1 and 4 show other combinations ✗

So (A), (B) and (C) are correct.

optionAnalysis.reason: Select RA on Mux_A and RB on Mux_B: both ALU operands are registers.
Select RA and the immediate on Mux_B (or the immediate on Mux_A and RB): one register and one immediate.
Each multiplexer has its own 32-bit immediate input, so selecting the immediate on both gives two immediate operands.
The word "only" is false: (A) and (C) are also possible. This trap catches readers who assume the usual MIPS-style datapath where only the second operand can be an immediate.

cse-2025-1-cs-17.shortcut: Two independent 2-way choices ⇒ all four pairs {reg, imm} × {reg, imm} are possible; any option with "only" is therefore false.
pitfalls: Assuming, from the MIPS datapath, that only the second ALU input can take an immediate — this figure has an immediate input on both multiplexers.
Rejecting (C) because adding two constants is "useless" — the question asks what the hardware can do, not what a compiler would emit.
cse-2025-1-cs-17.verification: Count: 2 sources for Mux_A × 2 sources for Mux_B = 4 combinations, which exactly cover the reg–reg, reg–imm (both orders) and imm–imm cases listed in the table.

cse-2025-1-cs-18.approach: Use the subset construction (an $n$-state NFA always has an equivalent DFA with at most $2^n$ states) and the fact that a given automaton need not be minimal. Then mark each statement as possible/true or false.

steps.title: Subset construction bounds the DFA size
steps.body:
Each DFA state of the subset construction is a set of NFA states, and an $n$-element set has $2^n$ subsets. So there is always a DFA for $L$ with **at most $2^n$ states**.

Hence (C) "there exists a DFA with $\le 2^n$ states" is **true**.

steps.title: The given NFA need not be minimal
steps.body:
Nothing says the $n$-state NFA is the smallest one. Example with $n = 3$: the 3-cycle $q_0 \xrightarrow{a} q_1 \xrightarrow{a} q_2 \xrightarrow{a} q_0$ with all states accepting accepts $L = a^*$ (it is also a valid NFA).

But $a^*$ has a **1-state** NFA and a **1-state** DFA (one accepting state with an $a$-loop), and $1 < 3$.

So (A) "may have an NFA with $< n$ states" and (B) "may have a DFA with $< n$ states" are both **true** (they only claim possibility).

steps.title: Statement (D) contradicts (C)
steps.body:
(D) claims **every** DFA for $L$ has $> 2^n$ states. The subset-construction DFA has $\le 2^n$ states, so it is a counter-example (and in the $a^*$ example a 1-state DFA exists, $1 \le 2^3 = 8$).

(D) is **false**, and it is the only false statement.

optionAnalysis.reason: True statement (so not chosen): the given $n$-state NFA may be non-minimal, e.g. a 3-state NFA for $a^*$ while a 1-state NFA exists.
True statement: a DFA can be smaller than a non-minimal NFA (1-state DFA for $a^*$ vs the 3-state NFA). "May" only needs one instance.
True statement: the subset construction always gives a DFA with at most $2^n$ states.
False statement: the subset-construction DFA has $\le 2^n$ states, so not every DFA has $> 2^n$ states.

cse-2025-1-cs-18.shortcut: Subset construction ⇒ some DFA has $\le 2^n$ states, so (C) is true and its negation-like claim (D) is false; "may have fewer" claims are always possible because the given NFA need not be minimal.
pitfalls: Reading the question as "which are TRUE" — it asks for the FALSE ones.
Thinking (B) is false because "DFAs are bigger than NFAs": the blow-up is only an upper bound; a DFA can be smaller than a non-minimal NFA.
Misreading $2^n$ as $2n$ (the superscript is easy to lose).
cse-2025-1-cs-18.verification: For the $a^*$ example with $n = 3$: NFA with 1 state ✓ (A), DFA with 1 state ✓ (B), $1 \le 8$ ✓ (C), and the 1-state DFA has $1 \not> 8$, refuting (D).

cse-2025-1-cs-19.approach: Every I/O call blocks the process (it goes to the I/O queue); when the I/O completes the process returns to the **ready** queue. So the answer is just the number of I/O calls executed.

steps.title: One I/O before the loop: scanf
steps.body: `scanf` is an input operation: running → I/O queue, and on completion I/O queue → **ready queue**. That is entry **1**.

steps.title: Twenty I/Os inside the loop: printf
steps.body:
The loop runs for $i = 0, 1, \dots, 19$, i.e. $20$ iterations. `x = x+20` is pure CPU work, but each `printf` is an output operation, so each iteration adds one more return to the ready queue:

$$1 + 20 = 21$$

steps.title: return 0 terminates
steps.body:
`return 0` ends the process (running → terminated); it does not enter the ready queue again. The initial admission is excluded by the question.

Total re-entries into the ready queue: **21**.

cse-2025-1-cs-19.shortcut: Ready-queue re-entries = number of blocking I/O calls = $1 + 20 = 21$.
pitfalls: Counting two entries per I/O because there are two context switches (one on the request, one on the return): the request moves the process to the I/O queue, not the ready queue.
Adding the initial entry (22) — the question explicitly excludes it.
Counting the loop as 21 iterations ($i$ from 0 to 20) — the condition is $i < 20$.
cse-2025-1-cs-19.verification: State path per I/O: running → waiting → ready → running. With 21 I/O calls this cycle happens 21 times; after the last printf the process runs to `return 0` and exits.

cse-2025-1-cs-20.approach: Count the complement: strings of length 5 with **no** two equal adjacent symbols are easy ($3 \cdot 2^4$); subtract from all $3^5$ strings.
concepts: Strings with no equal adjacent symbols

steps.title: All ternary strings of length 5
steps.body:
Each of the 5 positions can be $a$, $b$ or $c$:

$$3^5 = 243$$

steps.title: Strings with no two equal consecutive symbols
steps.body:
First symbol: 3 choices. Every later symbol must differ from the one before it: 2 choices each.

$$3 \times 2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 2 = 3 \times 2^4 = 48$$

steps.title: Subtract
steps.body:
Strings containing at least one of "aa", "bb", "cc":

$$243 - 48 = 195$$

pitfalls: Counting the 4 adjacent positions × 3 doubled letters × $3^3$ fillers $= 324$: this over-counts strings with several equal pairs (e.g. "aaaaa").
Using $2^5$ instead of $3 \cdot 2^4$ for the complement (the first symbol has 3 choices, not 2).
cse-2025-1-cs-20.verification: Recurrence check. Let $g_n$ = strings with no equal pair ($g_n = 3 \cdot 2^{n-1}$) and $w_n$ = strings with at least one. Appending a symbol: $w_n = 3w_{n-1} + g_{n-1}$ (any symbol after a "bad" string, or the repeated symbol after a "good" one). $w_1=0$, $w_2 = 0+3 = 3$, $w_3 = 9+6 = 15$, $w_4 = 45+12 = 57$, $w_5 = 171+24 = 195$ ✓.

cse-2025-1-cs-21.approach: Differentiable at $x = 1$ means continuous there **and** equal one-sided derivatives. The derivative condition gives $a$, continuity then gives $b$.

steps.title: Only x = 1 needs checking
steps.body: Both pieces are polynomials, so $f$ is differentiable everywhere except possibly at the joint $x = 1$.

steps.title: Match the derivatives at x = 1
steps.body:
Left piece: $\frac{d}{dx}(ax + b) = a$.

Right piece: $\frac{d}{dx}(x^3 + x^2 + 1) = 3x^2 + 2x$, which at $x = 1$ is $3 + 2 = 5$.

So $a = 5$.

steps.title: Continuity at x = 1 gives b
steps.body:
$f(1) = 1^3 + 1^2 + 1 = 3$ and the left limit is $a \cdot 1 + b = a + b$. Continuity: $a + b = 3$, so

$$b = 3 - a = 3 - 5 = -2$$

pitfalls: Using only continuity ($a + b = 3$) — one equation cannot fix $b$.
Differentiating $x^3 + x^2 + 1$ as $3x^2 + 2x + 1$ (the constant has derivative 0), which gives $a = 6$, $b = -3$.
cse-2025-1-cs-21.verification: With $a = 5$, $b = -2$: left value $5 - 2 = 3 = f(1)$ ✓, left slope $5 =$ right slope $3 + 2$ ✓.

cse-2025-1-cs-22.approach: This is Bayes' theorem: draw the two-stage probability tree (which coin, then two tosses), multiply along branches to get the joint probability of each way to see HH, and divide the fake-coin branch by the total.
cse-2025-1-cs-22.given: 5 coins: 4 regular ($P(H) = 0.5$), 1 fake ($P(H) = 1$). One coin is picked uniformly at random and tossed twice; the result is HH. Find $P(\text{fake} \mid HH)$.

steps.title: Priors: which coin was picked
steps.body: Picking uniformly from 5 coins: $P(F) = \frac15$ (fake), $P(R) = \frac45$ (regular).

steps.title: Likelihood of two heads for each coin
steps.body:
Tosses are independent given the coin:

- fake: $P(HH \mid F) = 1 \times 1 = 1$
- regular: $P(HH \mid R) = \frac12 \times \frac12 = \frac14$

steps.title: Total probability of HH
steps.body:
Multiply along each branch and add:

$$P(HH) = \tfrac15 \cdot 1 + \tfrac45 \cdot \tfrac14 = \tfrac15 + \tfrac15 = \tfrac25$$

steps.title: Apply Bayes' theorem
steps.body:
$$P(F \mid HH) = \frac{P(F)\,P(HH \mid F)}{P(HH)} = \frac{1/5}{2/5} = \frac12 = 0.50$$

Both branches contribute the same $\frac15$, so given HH the two explanations are equally likely.

cse-2025-1-cs-22.shortcut: Think in equally likely cases: each coin has 4 equally likely toss-pairs (20 cases in all). A regular coin shows HH in 1 of its 4; the fake coin shows HH in all 4. So HH happens in $4 \times 1 + 4 = 8$ cases, 4 of them fake: $4/8 = 0.5$.
pitfalls: Answering the prior $1/5 = 0.2$ — the two heads are evidence that must update it.
Using $P(HH \mid R) = \frac12$ (one toss) instead of $\frac14$ (two tosses).

cse-2025-1-cs-23.approach: fun() is bubble sort, and every swap of adjacent elements removes exactly one inversion. A fully descending array of 30 distinct values has every pair inverted, so swaps $= \binom{30}{2}$.

steps.title: Recognise the algorithm
steps.body: Pass $i$ compares $A[j], A[j+1]$ for $j = 0 \dots n-i-2$ and swaps when they are out of order — this is bubble sort. Pass $i$ makes $n-1-i$ comparisons.

steps.title: In a descending array every comparison swaps
steps.body: Pass 0 on $30, 29, \dots, 1$: the current maximum (30) is greater than every next element, so all $29$ comparisons swap and 30 moves to the end. The prefix left behind, $29, 28, \dots, 1$, is still descending, so the same happens in every pass: pass $i$ performs $n-1-i = 29-i$ swaps.

steps.title: Add the swaps of all passes
steps.body:
$$29 + 28 + \dots + 1 = \frac{29 \times 30}{2} = 435$$

Equivalently, each swap fixes one inversion and a descending array has $\binom{30}{2} = \frac{30 \times 29}{2} = 435$ inversions.

cse-2025-1-cs-23.shortcut: Bubble-sort swaps = number of inversions; reverse-sorted $n$ distinct keys have $n(n-1)/2$ inversions: $30 \cdot 29/2 = 435$.
pitfalls: Using $n^2/2 = 450$ or $n(n+1)/2 = 465$ instead of $n(n-1)/2$.
Counting passes ($29$) or comparisons of only the first pass instead of all swaps.
cse-2025-1-cs-23.verification: Small case $n = 3$ ([3,2,1]): pass 0 swaps twice → [2,1,3], pass 1 swaps once → [1,2,3]; total $3 = \binom32$ ✓, matching the formula.

cse-2025-1-cs-24.approach: Trace the pointer: `z` holds the address of `a`, that address is copied into `p`, and `*p = x` writes through it into `a` itself.

steps.title: foo receives a copy of the address
steps.body: `foo(z, b)` copies `z` into `p` (so `p = &a`) and `b` into `x` (`x = 25`). The statement `*p = x` stores $25$ at the address held in `p` — that is `a`.

steps.title: Print a
steps.body: Back in `main`, `a` is now $25$, so the program prints **25**.

cse-2025-1-cs-24.shortcut: Writing through a copied pointer changes the pointee: `*(&a) = 25` ⇒ prints 25.
pitfalls: Answering 20 by treating the call as "pass by value, nothing changes": the pointer is copied, but it still points to `a`.
Confusing which argument is stored: `*p = x` stores the value of `b` (25), not the old `a`.
cse-2025-1-cs-24.verification: Only one assignment touches `a` after initialisation: `*p = x` with `p == &a` and `x == 25`; hence `a == 25` at the `printf`.

cse-2025-1-cs-25.approach: A binary heap is a **complete** binary tree, so its height is forced: $h = \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$. Check by counting how many keys levels $0..h$ can hold.

steps.title: A heap has a fixed shape
steps.body: Whatever the key values, a binary (min-)heap is a **complete** binary tree: every level is full except possibly the last, which is filled from the left. So the height depends only on the number of keys, $n = 32$.

steps.title: Capacity of levels 0 to 4
steps.body:
Level $k$ of a complete binary tree holds up to $2^k$ nodes. Levels $0$ to $4$ hold at most

$$1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 = 2^5 - 1 = 31 \text{ keys.}$$

steps.title: The 32nd key starts level 5
steps.body:
$32 > 31$, so one key must go to level 5 (the leftmost slot, as the heap fills levels left to right). The deepest leaf is at depth 5:

$$h = \lfloor \log_2 32 \rfloor = 5$$

cse-2025-1-cs-25.shortcut: $h = \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$; $32 = 2^5$ is exactly one more than a full tree of height 4.
pitfalls: Using $\lceil \log_2 32 \rceil$ or $\log_2 32$ without checking the definition — it happens to match here, but $\lceil \log_2 n \rceil$ is wrong for e.g. $n = 31$ (height 4, not 5).
Counting levels (6) instead of edges (5); the question defines height in edges.
cse-2025-1-cs-25.verification: A full tree of height 5 has $2^6 - 1 = 63$ nodes, height 4 has 31: $31 < 32 \le 63$ ⇒ height 5 ✓.

animation.title: Keys per level in a 32-key heap

cse-2025-1-cs-26.approach: Split the 20-bit address into tag / line index / block offset for a direct-mapped cache; total tag storage = (tag bits) × (number of lines).
cse-2025-1-cs-26.given: Main memory $1\text{ MB} = 2^{20}$ B (20-bit address), cache $16\text{ KB} = 2^{14}$ B, block $16 = 2^4$ B, direct mapped, byte addressable.

steps.title: Block offset
steps.body: Block size $16 = 2^4$ bytes ⇒ **4** offset bits.

steps.title: Number of lines and index bits
Tag bits per line
steps.body: $$\text{tag} = 20 - 10 - 4 = 6 \text{ bits}$$

steps.title: Total tag storage
steps.body:
One tag per line:

$$6 \times 2^{10} \text{ bits} = 6144 \text{ bits}$$

This is option (A).

optionAnalysis.reason: 6-bit tag × $2^{10}$ lines.
8-bit tags would arise for a 4-way set-associative cache (2 fewer index bits); in a direct-mapped cache the tag is 6 bits.
$2^{12} = 4 \times 2^{10}$ means a 4-bit tag — the offset width was mistaken for the tag width.
$2^{14} = 16 \times 2^{10}$: a 16-bit tag (the whole block number), which is the fully associative case, or a confusion with the 16 KB data size.

pitfalls: Counting cache lines as $2^{14}$ (bytes) instead of $2^{14}/16 = 2^{10}$ blocks.
Using the fully associative tag (16 bits) for a direct-mapped cache.
cse-2025-1-cs-26.verification: Bit budget: $6 + 10 + 4 = 20$ ✓. Each tag identifies which of $2^{20}/2^{14} = 64 = 2^6$ memory blocks share a line ✓.

cse-2025-1-cs-27.approach: `ADD R1, #25` needs three fields: opcode, one register, immediate. Give the opcode and register the minimum bits they need; everything left of the 32 bits is for the immediate.

steps.title: Opcode bits
steps.body: 50 instruction types need $\lceil \log_2 50 \rceil = 6$ bits, since $2^5 = 32 < 50 \le 64 = 2^6$.

steps.title: Register field
steps.body: 64 registers need $\log_2 64 = 6$ bits. The instruction names one register (R1 is both source and destination).

steps.title: Immediate field
steps.body:
$$32 - 6 - 6 = 20 \text{ bits}$$

This is option (B).

optionAnalysis.reason: 16 is the familiar MIPS I-type immediate; here nothing forces a second register field, so the immediate can take all 20 remaining bits.
6 (opcode) + 6 (register) + 20 (immediate) = 32.
22 leaves only 10 bits for opcode + register, e.g. 5 + 5 — but 5 bits encode only 32 < 50 types and 32 < 64 registers.
24 leaves only 8 bits, which cannot hold a 6-bit opcode and a 6-bit register number.

pitfalls: Taking $\lfloor \log_2 50 \rfloor = 5$ opcode bits (only 32 opcodes).
Reserving two or three register fields as in a generic three-address format; this instruction uses only R1.
cse-2025-1-cs-27.verification: Field sum $6 + 6 + 20 = 32$ ✓; 6 bits give 64 ≥ 50 opcodes ✓ and exactly 64 register numbers ✓.

cse-2025-1-cs-28.approach: Simulate the two processors event by event (t = 0, then each time a processor becomes free), each time giving the free processor the waiting process with the highest priority **in that processor's own order**. All arrivals are at 0, so waiting time = start time.

steps.title: t = 0: both processors free
steps.body:
$M_1$'s top choice is $P_1$; $M_2$'s top choice is $P_2$. ($P_1$ cannot go to $M_2$ because $P_2$, higher on $M_2$'s list, is waiting; likewise $P_2$ cannot take $M_1$ ahead of $P_1$.)

$M_1$: $P_1$ runs $0 \to 20$. $M_2$: $P_2$ runs $0 \to 16$.

steps.title: t = 16: M2 becomes free
steps.body: Waiting: $P_3, P_4$. On $M_2$'s list $P_3 > P_4$, so $P_3$ runs $16 \to 16 + 25 = 41$ on $M_2$.

steps.title: t = 20: M1 becomes free
steps.body: Only $P_4$ is waiting, so $P_4$ runs $20 \to 20 + 10 = 30$ on $M_1$. Everything finishes by $t = 41$.

steps.title: Average waiting time
steps.body:
All processes arrive at $t = 0$, so waiting time = start time:

| $P_1$ | $P_2$ | $P_3$ | $P_4$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0 | 16 | 20 |

$$\bar W = \frac{0 + 0 + 16 + 20}{4} = \frac{36}{4} = 9.00 \text{ ms}$$

optionAnalysis.reason: Needs a total wait of 35 ms; the schedule forced by the priority rules gives 36.
Needs a total wait of only 26 ms, but no processor is free before $t = 16$, so the two processes not started at 0 wait at least $16 + 20 = 36$ ms in total.
Needs a total wait of 30 ms; the free instants are forced (16 on $M_2$, 20 on $M_1$), so the two later processes always wait $16 + 20 = 36$ ms.

cse-2025-1-cs-28.shortcut: Each machine takes its top process at 0 ($P_1$ on $M_1$, $P_2$ on $M_2$); $M_2$ frees first at 16 and takes $P_3$; $P_4$ gets $M_1$ at 20. Waits $16 + 20 = 36$, average $9$.
pitfalls: Using one global priority order instead of each processor's own list.
Computing average turnaround $(20 + 16 + 41 + 30)/4 = 26.75$ instead of waiting time.
Letting a processor stay idle or assigning $P_3$ to $M_1$ at 20 — $M_2$ is already free at 16 and takes it then.
cse-2025-1-cs-28.verification: Independent check: the processors become free only at 16 ($M_2$) and 20 ($M_1$), so whichever two processes start second wait 16 and 20; total $36$, average $9.00$. Turnaround check: finishes 20, 16, 41, 30 minus bursts 20, 16, 25, 10 gives waits 0, 0, 16, 20 ✓.

cse-2025-1-cs-29.approach: A correct TRC query must (1) range the output tuple $p$ over the relation that has $\mathit{pname}$, (2) range $t$ over the relation that has $\mathit{tname}$, and (3) **join** them on $\mathit{tid}$. Check each option for these three things.

steps.title: Which variable ranges over which relation
steps.body:
$\mathit{pname}$ is an attribute of $\mathit{players}$ only and $\mathit{tname}$ of $\mathit{teams}$ only. So the query needs $p \in \mathit{players}$ and $t \in \mathit{teams}$.

(B) and (D) have $p \in \mathit{teams}$ and $t \in \mathit{players}$, so $p.\mathit{pname}$ and $t.\mathit{tname}$ do not exist — both are ill-formed.

steps.title: The join condition
steps.body:
A player plays for team MI exactly when **his own** team tuple has name MI: $\exists t \in \mathit{teams}$ with $p.\mathit{tid} = t.\mathit{tid}$ and $t.\mathit{tname} = \text{'MI'}$.

(C) drops $p.\mathit{tid} = t.\mathit{tid}$: its condition "$\exists t$ with $t.\mathit{tname} = \text{'MI'}$" does not mention $p$ at all, so it returns **every** player's name whenever a team called MI exists.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body:
Only (A) has the right ranges **and** the join:

$$\{\, p.\mathit{pname} \mid p \in \mathit{players} \land \exists t\,(t \in \mathit{teams} \land p.\mathit{tid} = t.\mathit{tid} \land t.\mathit{tname} = \text{'MI'})\,\}$$

optionAnalysis.reason: $p$ over players, $t$ over teams, joined on $\mathit{tid}$, filtered on $\mathit{tname} = \text{'MI'}$ — exactly the MI players.
Relations swapped: $p \in \mathit{teams}$ has no $\mathit{pname}$ and $t \in \mathit{players}$ has no $\mathit{tname}$.
No join $p.\mathit{tid} = t.\mathit{tid}$: the existential is independent of $p$, so all players are returned if any team is named MI (and none otherwise).
Both errors at once: swapped relations and no join condition.

cse-2025-1-cs-29.shortcut: Eliminate swapped ranges (B, D), then keep the option with $p.\mathit{tid} = t.\mathit{tid}$ (A).
pitfalls: Picking (C) because it "mentions MI": without the join it is a cross-product test that ignores which team the player belongs to.
cse-2025-1-cs-29.verification: Relational-algebra equivalent of (A): $\pi_{\mathit{pname}}(\mathit{players} \bowtie \sigma_{\mathit{tname} = \text{'MI'}}(\mathit{teams}))$ — the natural join on $\mathit{tid}$ is the $p.\mathit{tid} = t.\mathit{tid}$ condition.
